displayQuote: No two persons ever read the same book

meta.title: Who really said "No two persons ever read the same book"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Edmund Wilson — but not in those words. What he actually wrote, in the preface to 'The Triple Thinkers', is longer and better: one can never read the book the author wrote, and never read the same book twice.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No two persons ever read the same book'?
meta.ogDescription: The right author, the wrong sentence. Wilson's real line is in the preface to The Triple Thinkers — and it says something sharper than the slogan.

answer.label: Right author, polished wording
answer.authorDates: 1895–1972 · American critic and man of letters
answer.sourceLine: The idea is genuinely Edmund Wilson’s, and the source is locatable: the preface to The Triple Thinkers, his 1938 collection of essays on literary subjects. What he wrote there is longer than the slogan — that one can never read the book the author actually wrote, and never read the same book twice. Nobody has produced a Wilson text containing the seven-word version people quote.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Triple Thinkers: Twelve Essays on Literary Subjects

source.excerpt: In a sense, one can never read the book that the author originally wrote, and one can never read the same book twice.
trail: The question has a public answer with a public trail: someone asked Literature Stack Exchange where to find the line, and the accepted answer sends them to the preface of The Triple Thinkers, p. ix, for the sentence above — noting the popular version is ‘likely to be a slight variation’ of it the question ↗.

Wikiquote lists the preface sentence with a page citation and does not list the seven-word version as a sourced Wilson quotation — a useful negative result, because Wilson is a heavily indexed writer Wikiquote ↗.

The short form is everywhere in quote databases with no citation attached, and is sometimes traced no further back than a 1971 newspaper piece quoting Wilson at second hand. That is a report of a saying, not a text.
source.excerptNote: Wilson’s actual sentence, quoted briefly for identification. Notice it does two things the slogan does not: it puts the author’s lost book on the table, and it says you cannot even repeat the experience yourself.

sourceLink.text: Literature Stack Exchange — where the line comes from

source.rightsNote: In copyright. The Triple Thinkers was published in 1938 and revised in 1948, and Edmund Wilson died in 1972 — so the book remains protected in the United States and, on a life-plus-seventy term, across the UK and EU into the 2040s. The bare seven-word aphorism is too short and too anonymous in origin for anyone to police, but Wilson’s real sentence is a copyrighted text: quote it briefly with the title and page, and do not treat a 1938 critic as public-domain wallpaper. This is not legal advice.

author.heading: About Edmund Wilson
author.metaLine: 1895–1972 · American critic, essayist and literary journalist
author.bio: Edmund Wilson was the most influential American literary critic of the twentieth century — a friend and editor of Fitzgerald, the author of Axel’s Castle and To the Finland Station, and for decades the reviewer whose verdict decided reputations. He wrote for readers rather than for the seminar room, which is why so many of his sentences survive as sayings. It is also why they get shortened: a Wilson paragraph is easy to compress and hard to improve.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: There is no villain here and no wrong author. What there is, is a critic’s sentence that got sanded into a bookmark — and a slogan now quoted, in quotation marks, as though it were a text.

items.why: The thought is his and the source is findable: the preface to The Triple Thinkers. This is not a misattribution; it is a misquotation.
No Wilson text has been produced containing ‘No two persons ever read the same book.’ It is a paraphrase that hardened into a quotation, complete with quote marks it has not earned.
Wilson’s first clause is about the writer: the book the author meant is unreachable too. The slogan keeps only the reader-relativism half, which is the comfortable half.

Reference works sometimes attach the short version to a 1971 newspaper article quoting Wilson. Even if accurate, that records a critic saying something in conversation — it is not a page you can open.

misattribution.truthLine: Edmund Wilson, genuinely — but the sentence he wrote is longer, and it is in the preface to The Triple Thinkers the sourced wording ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Every reader has had the experience the line describes — recommending a beloved book to a friend who comes back baffled, or rereading something at forty that meant something else entirely at twenty. It names a private, slightly embarrassing fact about reading.

It is also a permission slip. If no two people read the same book, then your reading is not a wrong answer waiting to be corrected by someone with a doctorate, which is a very appealing thing for a famous critic to have conceded.
context.detailsSummary: Why the longer version is the better one
detailsBody: Wilson wrote the preface to introduce twelve essays about how criticism works. The point is methodological: no reading is neutral, including his own.
The clause about the author’s original book is the one worth keeping. It says the writer’s intended object is lost to everyone, the writer included.
‘One can never read the same book twice’ is the harder claim — not that we differ from each other, but that we differ from ourselves.
The seven-word version is more quotable and says less. That trade happens to a lot of good sentences on the way to becoming tote bags.
context.pull: Not that we differ from each other. That we differ from ourselves.
